sections.skill: Choose a savings product by safety, liquidity, and return

questions.prompt: What is a certificate of deposit (CD)?

choices.text: A stock that pays the same fixed dividend to owners every month
A checking account with free checks
A loan that a bank gives to students
A deposit left for a set term at a usually fixed rate

questions.correct_answer: A deposit left for a set term at a usually fixed rate
questions.intro: A certificate of deposit (CD) is a bank or credit union deposit that you agree to leave for a set term, such as 6 months or 5 years. In return, it usually pays a fixed rate. Taking money out before the term ends usually costs an early-withdrawal penalty. CDs are insured deposits up to the legal limit.
questions.feedback: A CD is a time deposit with a set term and usually a fixed rate.
questions.topic: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts

misconceptions.A: Confuses a CD with a stock
misconceptions.C: Confuses a CD with a loan

questions.prompt: Max's $5,000 CD pays 4.5% simple interest. The penalty for early withdrawal is 90 days of interest. About how much is the penalty (use 365 days in a year)?
questions.intro: Early-withdrawal penalties are often stated as a number of days or months of interest. Penalty ≈ principal × rate × (days ÷ 365).

questions.prompt: Which statement about a money market DEPOSIT account (at a bank) and a money market FUND (at a brokerage) is TRUE?

choices.text: Both are FDIC insured
Only the fund is FDIC insured
Only the deposit account is FDIC insured
Neither can ever lose value, because both are offered by banks

questions.correct_answer: Only the deposit account is FDIC insured
questions.intro: A money market deposit account is a bank deposit, insured up to the legal limit. A money market fund is a mutual fund that invests in short-term debt. It aims to keep a stable value but is not FDIC insured and can, rarely, lose value.
questions.feedback: The bank account is a deposit (insured); the fund is an investment (not FDIC insured).

questions.prompt: Lily will need $3,000 for college fees in exactly 12 months, and she will not touch it before then. Which choice fits best?

choices.text: A 5-year CD with a large early-withdrawal penalty
A stock fund, for the highest possible return
Her checking account, which pays no interest
A 12-month CD at an insured bank

questions.correct_answer: A 12-month CD at an insured bank
questions.intro: Match the product to when you need the money. Money needed on a known date can go in a CD whose term ends by that date. Money you may need any time belongs in a savings account.
questions.feedback: A 12-month CD matches the timeline and keeps the money safe.

sections.skill: Liquidity: how quickly money can be used
sections.relationship: Choosing a savings product depends on trading access (liquidity) against return.

questions.prompt: What does "liquidity" mean in personal finance?

choices.text: How quickly money can be used without losing value
How much interest an account pays each year, as a percent
How much water a bank uses
How large an account balance is

questions.correct_answer: How quickly money can be used without losing value
questions.intro: Liquidity describes how easily and quickly something can be turned into cash you can spend, without losing value. Cash and checking are very liquid; a house is not.
questions.feedback: Liquidity = quick access without loss of value.

questions.prompt: Rosa splits $4,000 into four CDs of $1,000 each, maturing in 1, 2, 3, and 4 years. What is this strategy called?

choices.text: A CD ladder
A CD pyramid scheme
A savings sweep
A money market account

questions.intro: A CD ladder spreads money across CDs with different maturity dates. One CD matures each year, giving regular access to part of the money, and maturing CDs can be reinvested at current rates.

questions.prompt: Series I savings bonds have a rate that adjusts with inflation. What is the main purpose of that feature?

choices.text: To help savings keep up with rising prices
To guarantee the bond doubles in value every single year
To make the bond a stock investment
To avoid any holding period

questions.correct_answer: To help savings keep up with rising prices
questions.intro: I bonds are U.S. savings bonds whose rate includes an inflation adjustment that changes every six months. They must be held at least 12 months, and cashing them in before 5 years costs the last 3 months of interest.
questions.feedback: The inflation-adjusted rate helps protect purchasing power.
